UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                     BEFORE THE
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                           )
Revisions to the Blanket Certificate Program               )                      Docket No. RM25-12-001
                                                           )

                                           COMMENTS OF
                                        ENCHANTED ROCK, LLC

         Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC” or “Commission”)

May 21, 2026, Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“NOPR”)1 in the above-captioned proceeding,

Enchanted Rock, LLC (“ERock”)2 hereby respectfully submits these comments (“Comments”) for

the Commission’s consideration.

         ERock supports the Commission’s proposed modernization of the blanket certificate

program because, inter alia, the proposed revisions would: (i) update cost limits to better reflect

natural gas infrastructure construction costs,3 (ii) preserve streamlined authorization pathways for

routine and well-understood projects,4 (iii) remove cost limits for eligible expansions of existing

compressor stations within the existing fence line while retaining prior notice review and

environmental safeguards,5 and (iv) better align natural gas infrastructure development with the

speed-to-power needs of large load customers.6




1
  Revisions to the Blanket Certificate Program, Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, 195 FERC ¶ 61,128 (2026).
2
  ERock is a leading developer, owner, and operator of onsite power generation headquartered in Houston, Texas. As
of December 31, 2025, ERock had approximately 1,000 MW of installed capacity across more than 400 operational
sites nationwide, delivering 99.999% combined reliability. ERock’s natural gas generators support data centers,
utilities, manufacturers, healthcare systems, government organizations, and other critical infrastructure customers by
helping address grid constraints, interconnection delays, and outage risks. Through its integrated development,
engineering, construction, operations, and maintenance capabilities, ERock delivers bridge power, backup power,
flexible capacity, and grid support services that help customers address interconnection delays, improve resiliency,
and strengthen grid reliability.

                                                          1
          These reforms are particularly important to enable on-site, gas-fired generation to serve

large load customers before transmission upgrades are built to serve them, reduce near-term strain

on the transmission system, support more efficient use of existing energy infrastructure, and

ultimately advance long-term ratepayer affordability. For these reasons, and the reasons described

further herein, ERock supports the NOPR reforms discussed in these Comments and respectfully

urges the Commission to promulgate a final rule adopting those reforms as soon as practicable.

I.       COMMENTS

         A.       ERock Generally Supports the NOPR, Which Will Help Address Speed-to-Power
                  Challenges Faced by Large Load Customers

         Large load customers increasingly prioritize speed-to-power as the determinative factor in

project siting, a trend accelerated by the global artificial intelligence (“AI”) race that underpins

U.S. economic competitiveness and national security priorities.7 Ensuring that AI infrastructure

does not face offshoring risks due to domestic power constraints is of paramount national

importance. Providing timely access to reliable, dispatchable generation—enabled by FERC-

jurisdictional natural gas infrastructure—is vital to meeting this challenge.8 Expanding and

optimizing such infrastructure at a pace commensurate with commercial schedules is necessary

not only to maintain bulk power system reliability, but also to secure the foundational energy

resources required to sustain U.S. leadership in the global AI landscape.9

the need for stable and predictable rules that encourage infrastructure investment and business confidence in the AI

9
  See, e.g., Comments of Enchanted Rock, LLC, Docket No. ER26-247-000, at 2–4 (Nov. 14, 2025) (discussing speed-
to-power, transmission constraints, and resource adequacy risks for large-load facilities); Reply Comments of
Enchanted Rock, LLC, Docket No. RM26-4-000, at 4–5 (Dec. 5, 2025).


                                                          2
         A central constraint affecting the timely development of large-scale energy infrastructure

is the ability of critical load facilities, such as AI data centers, to secure power as quickly and

reliably as possible. As demand accelerates, permitting bottlenecks associated with securing

incremental pipeline capacity will become increasingly acute, creating severe resource adequacy

and project deployment risks.10 The NOPR offers a pragmatic, necessary mechanism to alleviate

these timing constraints by directly addressing the mismatch between lengthy pipeline permitting

cycles and large load customers’ “speed-to-power” requirements. Critically, facilitating the

efficient expansion of natural gas infrastructure—including compressor station capacity—can also

complement the existing and planned transmission system by enabling on-site dispatchable

generation that reduces the immediate need for new transmission buildout, thereby supporting the

efficient utilization of the transmission system.

        More specifically, ERock supports the NOPR’s proposed increases to the blanket certificate

cost limits to $30 million for automatic authorization projects11 and $86 million for prior notice

projects.12 Further, ERock supports the NOPR’s proposed removal of cost limits for eligible

expansions of existing compressor stations within the station’s existing fence line, which

represents a practical and low-impact approach to streamlining infrastructure upgrades that can

unlock meaningful, additional gas transportation capacity.13 Moreover, the accompanying

proposed requirements for detailed air quality data and noise mitigation serve as effective

safeguards to ensure that these projects proceed responsibly.14

                                                       3
            Expanding blanket certificate eligibility in the manner proposed in the NOPR would allow

more routine, well-understood infrastructure upgrades to proceed without the administrative

burdens and extended timelines associated with a case-specific Natural Gas Act Section 7(c)

proceeding.15 The NOPR’s proposed changes would therefore better align gas delivery

infrastructure development with the upstream generation and downstream load requirements that

such infrastructure serves. Indeed, modernizing these cost limits and exempting eligible

compressor station expansions would reduce regulatory burdens on low-impact, routine projects

while appropriately balancing environmental and stakeholder interests. The Commission should

finalize these proposed reforms expeditiously.

           B.       A Final Rule Adopting the NOPR’s Proposed Reforms Would Enhance Speed-to-
                    Power, Reduce Permitting Delays, and Support Efficient Use of Existing Energy
                    Infrastructure

           The electric sector’s ability to deliver speed-to-power through modular, dispatchable

generation depends in part on FERC’s ability to promptly certify new natural gas infrastructure.

Aligning authorization timelines for routine, well-understood gas infrastructure projects with the

pace of large load growth is functionally necessary to prevent timeline mismatches that delay or

prevent the realization of generation and load projects under development. Further, enabling the

predictable deployment of dispatchable generation—supported by expedited pipeline and

compressor station upgrade approvals via the blanket certificate program—can advance long-term

ratepayer affordability as these dispatchable resources eventually transition into the utility’s supply

stack at a substantially depreciated net book value.

           If approved, higher cost thresholds for automatic authorization and prior notice projects

would allow more critical pipeline enhancement projects—including compressor station



15
     15 U.S.C. § 717f(c) (2024).


                                                   4
 expansions that can unlock additional gas transportation capacity—to qualify under the blanket

certificate program, thereby minimizing burdensome delays triggered by lengthy permitting

timelines.16 By allowing such expansions to proceed through prior notice review regardless of cost,

the NOPR would facilitate practical capacity additions that make more efficient use of existing

natural gas infrastructure and reduce the need for more disruptive greenfield pipeline development.

         Indeed, aligning gas pipeline infrastructure development with large load growth and

associated commercial schedules is necessary to ensure that critical energy infrastructure is ready

and available when customer demand materializes. Otherwise, viable projects may be delayed,

relocated, or fail to materialize, with corresponding adverse impacts to economic development,

grid reliability, and national energy security. Ensuring that targeted pipeline upgrades can be

authorized and constructed in step with associated load growth is essential to meeting the country’s

increasing energy demand.

         ERock further supports the NOPR’s proposed streamlining of routine natural gas

infrastructure upgrades because those reforms would help address circumstances in which peak

deliverability, rather than average annual throughput, is the limiting constraint.17 For instance,

large load customers and on-site generation providers may require the ability to deliver significant

quantities of natural gas during critical operating periods even if average usage appears more

modest.18 The NOPR would help address this peak-deliverability constraint because its proposed

cost-limit increases, proposed removal of cost limits for eligible in-fenceline compressor station

   For example, ERock has observed gas-deliverability limitations imposed by local distribution companies during
recent winter storms that prevented certain industrial, transportation-service, and critical-infrastructure customers
from operating during peak conditions. ERock has also observed otherwise viable data-center and large-load
opportunities stall or fail to reach final investment decision where available pipeline capacity was insufficient during
peak periods or where the infrastructure needed to resolve the constraint could not be permitted and constructed on
the customer’s speed-to-power schedule.


                                                           5
 expansions, and proposed harmonization of receipt- and delivery-point treatment for receipt points

eligible under automatic authorization would facilitate routine compressor additions, looping and

other eligible mainline work, receipt-point work, and other targeted system upgrades.19

         Further, ERock encourages the Commission to continue its engagement on gas-electric

coordination issues.20 While the blanket certificate program reforms proposed in the NOPR

represent a meaningful step toward improved gas-electric coordination, ERock encourages the

Commission to continue exploring additional opportunities to enhance the alignment between gas

infrastructure development and electric sector needs. As the interdependence between natural gas

supply and electric generation deepens—particularly in the context of serving large load facilities

with on-site, gas-fired generation—streamlined natural gas infrastructure permitting becomes an

increasingly important component of maintaining electric reliability.

         C.       ERock’s 366 MW Project in El Paso Electric’s Service Territory Demonstrates
                  How Bridge Generation Can Serve Large Loads While Protecting Ratepayers

         In further support of adopting the NOPR, ERock summarizes below its 366 MW natural

gas generation project under development in El Paso Electric’s (“EPE”) service territory in West

Texas (“McCloud Generation Facility”) as an operational example of how on-site, gas-fired

generation can address large load speed-to-power needs while delivering long-term benefits for

the utility, its ratepayers, and the surrounding community.21 ERock believes that a final rule

 adopting the reforms discussed in these Comments will enable more projects like the McCloud

Generation Facility to move forward because such reforms would enable a more rapid buildout of

key natural gas infrastructure.

        The McCloud Generation Facility will support a large-scale data center facility that

requires rapid access to reliable power on a timeline that traditional transmission and grid

expansion approaches cannot currently accommodate due to recurring interconnection bottlenecks

and multi-year delays. Specifically, the associated data center’s expected load increased from an

original ramp of approximately 220 MW to a peak of more than 440 MW by 2027 and potentially

1,000 MW by 2029.22 EPE selected the 366 MW McCloud Generation Facility in light of EPE’s

near-term system capacity constraints and the customer’s timing requirements.23 In light of such

constraints, the McCloud Generation Facility framework offers a practical and commercially

viable solution.

        Under the McCloud Generation Facility framework, ERock will construct a 366 MW on-

site generation facility using ultra-low-emission natural gas reciprocating engines, to be operated

on a 24/7/365 basis during an initial bridge period of up to five years (the “Bridge Period”).24 The

McCloud Generation Facility will be placed front-of-the-meter, dedicated to serving the large load

customer during this Bridge Period, with all capital expenditures and operational costs borne by

the data center customer to shield existing ratepayers from rate impacts.25 This Bridge Period

allows the data center to come online rapidly while permanent grid infrastructure upgrades are

Testimony of James Schichtl at 2–5, PUCT Docket No. 59076 (Dec. 8, 2025) (“Schichtl Direct Test.”).

 planned and constructed in the background.26 By operating separately from the bulk electric system

during this transitional phase, the McCloud Generation Facility addresses the immediate need for

speed-to-power without burdening the existing transmission system or requiring existing

ratepayers to absorb development costs.27

         After the Bridge Period, ERock’s generation assets are expected to transition into EPE’s

regulated rate base, at which point the utility can deploy the dispatchable capacity to serve its

broader customer base.28 Because the data center customer will have funded the initial capital

investment and absorbed years of depreciation during the Bridge Period, the utility would acquire

these assets at a significantly reduced net book value—resulting in a substantially lower cost per

kilowatt-hour for ratepayers compared to the construction of new generation resources. Assuming

a potentially useful life of no less than twenty years, such generation assets offer decades of

additional service to the grid after the Bridge Period concludes.29 This phased approach

demonstrates a synergistic model in which a large load customer’s need for speed-to-power

simultaneously creates a pathway to deliver cost-effective, reliable, dispatchable generation for the

broader grid over the long term.

         The NOPR’s proposed revisions to the blanket certificate program directly support the

viability of innovative frameworks like the McCloud Generation Facility framework. Natural gas

pipeline and compressor station infrastructure is essential to generation projects like the McCloud

                                                          8
 Generation Facility, which depend on reliable gas supply to fuel on-site generation.30 By

streamlining the authorization of routine gas infrastructure upgrades—particularly expansions

within the existing fence line of operational compressor stations—the NOPR would help ensure

that gas supply infrastructure keeps pace with the development timelines of generation projects

designed to serve large load customers. Under the updated blanket certificate program, projects

similar to the McCloud Generation Facility could benefit from expedited authorization of

associated pipeline infrastructure, improving commercial certainty and enabling more predictable,

replicable project development.

         Importantly, on-site gas-fired generation solutions like the McCloud Generation Facility

can complement the efficient utilization of the existing transmission system. Rather than requiring

immediate, large-scale transmission buildouts to serve new large loads, on-site generation fueled

by natural gas can serve as a bridge power solution that reduces near-term demand on the

transmission network. This approach allows transmission planners additional time to evaluate and

implement system upgrades in a measured, cost-effective manner—consistent with the

Commission’s broader objectives regarding the efficient utilization of existing transmission

infrastructure. The McCloud Generation Facility and similar frameworks also provide broader

economic development benefits, including accelerated local investment, expansion of the local tax

base, and job creation across construction, operations, and supporting industries.

         ERock continues to observe that modest infrastructure enhancements, including

compressor additions, looping and other routine system upgrades, can face lengthy approval

timelines even where they would unlock meaningful capacity with lower environmental and

                                                             9
 landowner impacts than greenfield pipeline development. A final rule adopting the NOPR’s

proposed reforms discussed in these Comments would meaningfully address these challenges.

Further, although the specific pipeline infrastructure upgrades associated with the McCloud

Generation Facility fall outside of FERC’s jurisdiction as intrastate facilities, ERock is exploring

other opportunities similar to the McCloud Generation Facility where the necessary pipeline

upgrades are within FERC’s jurisdiction. Streamlining the approval of routine, well-understood

infrastructure upgrades—such as compressor station expansions or system modifications—will

enable ERock and others to construct gas-fired, on-site power solutions to meet the needs of large

load customers in an accelerated manner.

II.    CONCLUSION

       ERock appreciates the Commission’s consideration of these Comments and the opportunity

to participate in this proceeding. For the reasons discussed above, ERock respectfully encourages

the Commission to finalize the proposed reforms discussed in these Comments expeditiously,

thereby facilitating the timely authorization of routine natural gas infrastructure projects that are

critical to meeting the nation’s growing energy needs.
